US$2 trillion was invested in clean energy globally last year, yet international public clean energy finance for developing countries amounted to just US$24.6 billion.
 
At today's Building Investment Plans to Unlock Climate Finance for Vulnerable Nations dialogue at #HLPF2026, I posed a simple question: Are SIDS and LDCs truly lacking bankable projects, or are we failing to recognize where value is being created?
 
The economics of the energy transition are increasingly compelling. Renewable electricity costs are projected to fall 30% by 2030, while electricity demand over the next five years is expected to grow 50% faster than over the previous decade. Capital is available. Demand is growing.
 
The opportunity is to connect the two.
 
That starts with better data. UNDP's satellite analysis identified 1.18 billion people living in energy poverty, around 60% more than those captured by conventional electricity access metrics. Better intelligence helps reveal hidden demand, reduce investment risk, and direct finance where it can deliver the greatest development impact.
 
It also means financing economic value creation. Clean energy should power industries, transport, agriculture, and digital economies that create jobs and strengthen resilience. This matters because manufacturing value added per capita in LDCs has increased by more than 40% since 2015, yet it remains far below the global average.
 
It also requires the right conditions for private investment. With around 80% of public clean energy finance coming as debt and only 5% supporting risk mitigation, countries need policy reform, blended finance, and tools like UNDP’s Energy Finance Innovation Labs to build investable pipelines and reduce risk.
 
Investment plans become bankable pipelines when we stop financing energy as a standalone asset and start financing the economic value it unlocks.
 
That is UNDP 's role: helping countries build the institutions, markets, and investment ecosystems that turn clean energy into jobs, industries, resilience, and long-term development.
 
My thanks to SEforALL and the Governments of Australia, Barbados, Fiji, and Tuvalu for convening this timely dialogue ahead of Pre-COP31 and for advancing the broader conversation on unlocking climate finance for vulnerable countries in the lead-up to COP31.
